title: MA9-04734
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Haiti, is claiming refugee protection under section 96 and paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (the IRPA). The Minister of Public Safety, hereinafter called the Minister, intervened in this claim and requested that the claimant be excluded, under section 98 of the IRPA, from the United Nations' Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees under Article 1F(b) of the Convention.2 Identity
The claimant's identity was established to the panel's satisfaction by means of the identity documents on file.3 SUMMARY OF FACTS

According to the Minister's evidence, while the claimant was living in the United States, he was arrested on XXXX XXXX, 2009, and accused of "burglary of an unoccupied dwelling, second degree felony."4 According to the evidence, the claimant was arrested while in the middle of committing a burglary. Exhibit M-1, at pages 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11, contains a very specific account of the XXXX XXXX, 2009, events.

The claimant testified about these events. He admitted that he entered his friends' home to steal; he admitted that he stole a television and other objects and that he put them in his car, which was parked a little further away. He re-entered the apartment, and it was at that point that he was caught by his friends, who were returning home. He admitted that he first fled and that he then stopped and faced his friends, explaining to them that he had stolen from their home. He denied that he entered by breaking in-he stated that his friends' apartment door had been broken for an undetermined period of time and that the way to enter the home was by using a screwdriver that was located in a flower pot beside the front door.

The police report paints a slightly different picture of the situation. The screwdriver did not belong to the victims because, according to Exhibit M-1, page 12, the two victims' DNA was not on the screwdriver, nor were their fingerprints, so the screwdriver did not belong to the two victims. This contradicts the claimant's version.
According to the Minister's evidence, the claimant never appeared in order to face justice following that arrest and, consequently, an arrest warrant was issued against him on XXXX XXXX, 2009.

The claimant explained that he left the United States on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, that he did not wait for the judicial proceedings, and that he evaded justice because he did not have any status in the United States; he was surely going to be deported to Haiti, and since he feared for his life in Haiti, he decided to come to Canada to claim refugee protection to be protected.

The Minister stated that if the claimant's offence had been committed in Canada, it would amount to the offence described in paragraph 348 (1) of the Criminal Code of Canada, that is, breaking and entering with intent, committing offence or breaking out. In Canada, this offence is punishable by imprisonment for life.5 ANALYSIS Did the claimant commit a crime?

Given the claimant's confession, I am of the opinion that the Minister's evidence and the claimant's confession about part of the events is overwhelming evidence that the claimant committed the crime for which he was arrested. I do not believe his version of the facts, namely, that the screwdriver was already in a flower pot near the door and that it was often used by the people because the door was broken. I accept the Minister's version, that is, that the screwdriver was a tool that served to break in to the victims' home. Furthermore, according to Exhibit M-1, the victims' neighbour heard noise and, I cite: "I heard noise next door, looked out and saw a person wearing a hood walking away from the apartment. This noise was this person breaking into the apartment next door."

Therefore, I am of the opinion that the claimant committed a crime that, had he committed it in Canada, would have been breaking and entering with intent, committing offence or breaking out. Is it a serious crime?

Although jurisprudence, in certain cases, has allowed for the notion of serious crime to be interpreted as the notion of serious criminality in the context of inadmissibility, according to section 36 of the IRPA, not all crimes for which the Act sets out a maximum term of imprisonment of at least ten years will be considered serious crimes under Article 1F(b) of the Convention, that is, in the context of exclusion. The panel must examine all of the circumstances of the case, including the nature of the crime committed.

The Federal Court proposed criteria for assessing the seriousness of a crime in Jayasekara:6 I believe there is a consensus among the courts that the interpretation of the exclusion clause in Article1F(b) of the Convention, as regards the seriousness of a crime, requires an evaluation of the elements of the crime, the mode of prosecution, the penalty prescribed, the facts and the mitigating and aggravating circumstances underlying the conviction. I will therefore analyze the act committed by the claimant in light of each criterion. Elements of the crime

Breaking and entering with intent, committing offence or breaking out is an offence against property, not an offence against a person. No violence against a person was committed in this case; no one was injured. Mode of prosecution
This criterion is not relevant in this case because the offence in question was not a hybrid offence. Penalty prescribed
The maximum penalty prescribed for this offence is imprisonment for life-an indication of the seriousness of this crime.

In his argument, the Minister reminded me that one of the objectives of Article 1F(b) of the Convention is to prevent perpetrators of criminal activity from fleeing justice, and the Minister submits that that is the case for the claimant, who fled justice: he did not appear to face the proceedings. However, he explained that he fears for his life in Haiti, that he knew perfectly well that, for all practical purposes, appearing before the justice system amounted to being deported to Haiti (and I have no doubt about that), and that that is why he came to Canada and claimed refugee protection immediately. I took that into account as well.

The Minister reminded me that the standard of proof is that of a "serious reason for considering." I reminded the Minister that this standard applies to fact-finding and not to assessing the seriousness of the crime.

The Minister asked me to consider as an aggravating circumstance the fact that the claimant did not appear for his appearance and that there was an arrest warrant against him. I considered this element. However, I must also consider the reasons he did not appear at his appearance, that is, his fear of persecution and his fear of being killed upon a return to Haiti, and that substantially mitigates the circumstance.

The Minister asked me to consider as an aggravating circumstance the fact that the claimant did not declare his run-ins with the American justice system in his Personal Information Form (PIF). This consideration is not linked to the commission of the offence; I cannot consider it as an aggravating circumstance. Mitigating circumstances

I considered a mitigating circumstance the fact that, after trying to flee on foot from where the offence was committed, the claimant stopped running and decided to face his friends, who are the victims in this case. He confessed everything to them right there; he told them that he had stolen their television and that the television was currently in his car. He waited for the police officers to arrive, and he spontaneously recounted his wrongful act. I cite the Minister's documentary evidence, at Exhibit M-1, page 7, where the police officer states: I made contact with XXXX who appeared upset and began to cry and beg for forgiveness. He then spontaneously uttered that he broke into his friends' residence, stole a TV and placed it inside his vehicle which he parked one street away. He repeatedly stated that he was sorry for what happened. I read XXXX his Miranda Rights he advised that he understood them and wished to waive them. I asked him why he was there, he stated that he came to steal the TV because he had recently lost his job and has no money to care for his family, he advised that he wanted to return the items he stole from his friends and said that his car was parked near the intersection of XXXX Avenue and XXXX Avenue. He then handed me the keys to the XXXX. XXXX signed a consent to search for the XXXX.... I asked him if he knows why he was there, he advised that he knows why. XXXX stated that he knew that it was wrong of him to steal the television but he did it because he just lost his job. He advised that he recently had a child and he does not have any money to care for her. He advised that he had already pawned most of his personal belongings. He stated that he stole the TV so he could sell it at the pawn shop. XXXX advised that he knew that there was no one home at that time. He said he used a screwdriver to force open the front door. He entered and stole the TV and placed it in the back seat of his car. The report states that the total value of the theft was $860.

The Minister alleged that I may not consider the claimant's remorse because jurisprudence does not allow it to be considered, somewhat like we could not consider his rehabilitation. I am of the opinion that given the rather particular circumstances of the file, the remorse expressed by the claimant, he expressed it immediately at the scene: he acknowledged his guilt, he recognized that what he had done was wrong, he asked for forgiveness, he cried and he spontaneously recounted everything that he had done, at the scene, immediately after he committed the offence. He cooperated fully with the authorities at that point.

These are rather particular circumstances. The claimant stated that he knew that his friends, the victims, were not there that evening. Therefore, he had no intention of committing an act of violence or of attacking these people. He explained that he acted out of necessity; it was a bad choice, it was an obvious lack of judgment, but I do not note in the report a profoundly criminal state of mind. I sense that he was in a state of panic and, as he stated, he felt that there was no other way for him to support his child who had just been born (his daughter was born six days earlier, as confirmed in the child's passport), because he had lost his job and he had sold most of his goods. He saw no other way out than to do that. It was a bad choice; it was a crime. Was it a serious crime?
The rather particular circumstances of the incident are recounted in detail in the police report; they are mitigating circumstances that counterbalance the other elements that I considered here.

Consequently, after considering all of the evidence, I conclude that the crime that the claimant committed outside Canada, before arriving in Canada, is not a serious non-political crime under these particular circumstances. Consequently, the exclusion clause 1F(b) does not apply here. I will not exclude the claimant and I reject the Minister's request for exclusion. Inclusion
The claimant claimed refugee protection with other members of his family, his daughter XXXX XXXX XXXX, her sister XXXX XXXX XXXX, his mother XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and another sister, XXXX XXXX XXXX.

The claimant's mother comes from a much-politicized family> The claimant's parents were involved in political activities and were active in politics for several years, and the claimant had been surrounded by his parents' political activities since his childhood. His written narrative provides many details about the serious problems of persecution that persisted for several years. In the claimant's family, his mother and father were members of the Parti Convergence [convergence party], which was in opposition to the Parti Lavalas [Lavalas party]. They were members of a convergence group called OPL (Organisation du peuple en lutte) [struggling people's organization]; they were among the leaders of the group. The narrative is very detailed about the serious persecution to which the claimant's family members was subjected; among other things, XXXX XXXX mother, the female claimant XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, was raped and beaten. The claimant was also beaten; all of this happened before their departure for the United States in 2004.

Considering this situation, which is corroborated by specific and convincing documentary evidence from the claimants, including Exhibit D-12, the OPL membership card of XXXX XXXX, which was a certificate for XXXX XXXX XXXX. The documentary evidence on the persecution to which OPL members and, more specifically, women, are subjected by the government. This documentary evidence was submitted under Exhibit D-14 in a bundle. Several letters to corroborate the claimants' allegations were submitted under exhibits D-4 to D-7. All of these documents corroborate the testimony of the claimants, which was very credible during the hearing.

The documentary evidence on the risk run by people who are politically active, more specifically, the risk run by people who return to Haiti after leaving for several years, in particular, those who had left because they feared political persecution, indicates that these people are at risk upon their return.7
For these reasons, I determine that the claimants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, are "Convention refugees."

The female claimant XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of the United States; her father, who is her designated representative, stated that she had no fear of persecution in the United States and that she alleged no risk. For that reason, her refugee protection claim is rejected. (2001), c. 27, as amended. 2 The Convention may be found in Schedule 1 of the IRPA. 3 See Exhibit A-1: the Immigration documents in a bundle contain several of the claimant's identity cards. 4 See Exhibit M-1. 5 See Exhibit M-6, articles 322 and 348 of the Criminal Code of Canada. 6 Jayasekara v. Canada, 2008 FCA 454 at paragraph 44. 7 See package submitted under Exhibit A-1, Tab 1.8.
